title: Electron Auto-Update Trust Boundaries
html:
Electron Auto-Update Trust Boundaries

Electron auto-update attack surface

Treat an updater as a remote-code-execution boundary: it retrieves executable content, decides whether that content is newer and trusted, stages it locally, and hands it to an installer. Review the complete trust graph—release index, per-version metadata, artifact, detached signatures, embedded verification key, cache, temporary path, and installer—not only whether the final .app is signed.[1][2]

High-value tests

  • Rollback/replay: replay a previously valid manifest and its still-signed artifact. A signature authenticates its input but provides no freshness; the client must reject versions below a persistent monotonic floor unless an authenticated recovery policy explicitly authorizes the rollback.[2]
  • Metadata/artifact substitution: independently alter the version, URL, expected hash, artifact, and detached signature. Also try mixing a valid artifact/signature pair from one release with metadata for another. If the release metadata is unsigned, TLS or a signed final executable does not stop a compromised origin/CDN from changing the selection logic.[1][2]
  • Signed channel confusion: serve a legitimately signed alpha, beta, development, or debug build through the production feed. Reusing the same key and policy across environments lets the artifact pass a signer-only check; production identity/channel must be part of the authenticated policy or use a separate trust root.[2]
  • Temporary-file TOCTOU: determine whether verification opens a pathname and installation later reopens that pathname. If a local attacker can rename, replace, or redirect the staged object between those operations, the installer may consume bytes that were never verified. A mode-0700 staging directory narrows access but does not make the two operations atomic.[2]

Static and runtime triage can quickly locate these boundaries.[1][2]

npx asar extract /path/to/app.asar /tmp/app-src
rg -n 'autoUpdater|electron-updater|setFeedURL|latest\.yml|allowInsecureTLS|downgrade' /tmp/app-src
rg -n 'sha(256|512)|ed25519|verify|signature|version|mkdtemp|chmod|rename' /tmp/app-src
sudo fs_usage -w -f filesystem "$PID" | rg -i 'update|latest|\.ya?ml|\.zip|\.dmg|tmp'

During an authorized test, intercept the update check, archive every response, and mutate one field at a time. Then inspect the staging directory ownership/mode and trace file opens from download through installation. On macOS, continue with installer trust-boundary testing if the flow reaches a privileged helper, and review code-signing weaknesses rather than treating “signed” as a complete identity check.[2]

Expected binding and policy

A defensible design authenticates both selection metadata and artifact bytes. The SafeUpdater reference design demonstrates an embedded Ed25519 public key, signed manifests and artifacts, a signed message derived from SHA-256(file) plus the version, and a SHA-512 artifact digest stored in signed metadata; it is explicitly a research reference rather than a production-ready package.[1][2]

Verify that the target additionally provides these properties.[1][2]

  • uses an unambiguous signed representation that binds the artifact digest to its canonical version and release environment;
  • disables downgrade by default and enforces a minimum accepted version for authorized rollback;
  • separates production from non-production through distinct keys/channels or authenticated release-policy data; and
  • installs the already-verified open file (or an equivalent immutable handle/object) instead of resolving the same pathname again.

References

  • [1] Doyensec ElectronSafeUpdater reference implementation
  • [2] Electron SafeUpdater: Designing a Secure Electron Auto-Update Mechanism
